title: Three expressions (CCC 2700–2724)

cards: Noon, in a quiet church, three people in one pew. The first murmurs a prayer under her breath, beads sliding through her fingers.
The second has a small Bible open on his knee, reading one line, looking up, reading it again. The third isn't doing anything anyone could see. No book, no words.
Just sitting, eyes resting on the tabernacle. From the back of the church they look like three different things. The Catechism says they're three ways of doing one thing.

teach.b: First, vocal prayer: prayer with words, aloud or under the breath. Jesus himself taught one. In the Douay-Rheims: "Thus therefore shall you pray: Our Father who art in heaven."
We're bodies as well as spirits, the Catechism says, so prayer naturally comes out through the lips. But the words are meant to carry the heart, not replace it. That's the voice.
Second, meditation: the mind at work, a search to understand what God is asking. It usually leans on something: scripture, an icon, a prayer of the liturgy, the writings of the saints.
The Catechism names lectio divina, slow holy reading, and the rosary. The model is Mary after the shepherds leave: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart."
Thought, imagination, feeling and desire all get used. That's the mind. Third, contemplation.
The Catechism quotes Teresa of Avila: close sharing between friends, taking time to be alone with the one who loves us.
And it tells the story you met on day two hundred thirty-two, from the French village of Ars: a peasant who prayed before the tabernacle and said simply, I look at him, and he looks at me.
The Catechism calls contemplation a gaze of faith fixed on Jesus. That's the gaze.
Three expressions, one prayer; the same person might use all three in a single afternoon.

how: Catholics pray vocally with the Our Father, the Hail Mary and the prayers of the Mass; meditate through lectio divina and the mysteries of the rosary; and some practice silent contemplation, often in adoration before the Blessed Sacrament.

o: three set times of day for Catholic prayer
the three main parts of the Mass, in order

games.q: voice, mind, gaze — tap the pairs.
p: the voice, words carrying the heart
I look at him, and he looks at me

s: the Catechism treats vocal prayer as a lesser kind of prayer to grow out of
it points out that Jesus himself taught a prayer with words, and says the words should carry the heart.
Mary pondering in her heart is a picture of meditation
"Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart."
Teresa of Avila described contemplation as close sharing between friends
the Catechism quotes her: time alone with the one who loves us.

games.q: a peasant of Ars prays before the tabernacle. how does he describe what he does there?
o: he recites every prayer he knows.
he looks at him, and he looks at me.
he asks for a good harvest.
games.why: in his telling, it is looking, and being looked at. the Catechism calls contemplation a gaze of faith.

practice: Voice: say one line of a prayer you know, or of anything that matters to you, slowly, in a whisper. Mind: take one word from that line and turn it over; what does it ask of you today?
Gaze: then let the words go and rest your attention, the way the peasant of Ars did, looking and letting yourself be looked at.

wordCard.voice: Three expressions. In the Catechism: vocal prayer, meditation and contemplation, prayer with the voice, with the mind, and with the gaze.

orig.note: Latin: contemplation — the word the Western Church used for the third expression, the quiet gaze of prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: voice, mind, gaze. Three ways in, and all of them one prayer. See you tomorrow.
